newsitem.title: USA: GM CEO says needs competitive Canadian pact.
newsitem.headline: GM CEO says needs competitive Canadian pact.

text.p: General Motors Corp Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Jack Smith said Wednesday the automaker needs to negotiate a new labor pact in Canada that will allow it to improve its competitive position.
Speaking to reporters at GM's Technical Center, Smith said certain demands now on the table from the Canadian Auto Workers union prevent GM from gaining needed efficiences.
"We've got certain things that will cripple the company if we don't get fixed right," Smith said.

More than 21,000 CAW members are on strike over GM demands that it have the flexibility in a new labor contract to send more parts work to outside suppliers. GM, the least efficient of Detroit's Big Threee automakers, said it needs to shed workers and sell unprofitable operations to stay competitive.

"There's a couple (items) on the table that we need to work our way through, otherwise we will not be competitive. That's the focus, hopefully we can work out our differences," Smith said. He said it would be difficult for GM to be competitive in Canada if it were forced to keep two parts plants that are currently up for sale.

"These are businesses that our competitors are not in. And it's very difficult to compete against companies that pay much lower wages. We're much better off being able to let someone else run those businesses," he said.

However, Smith said he would be available to negotiate directly with CAW President Buzz Hargrove at the appropriate time. "I know Buzz. When our people say it's an appropriate time to go, I'm sure I'll be available," he said.
GM North American Operations President G. Richard Wagoner declined to predict when GM's U.S. assembly operations would be affected by parts shortages due to the Canadian strike.
Wagoner said he does not expect an immediate shutdown of U.S. assembly plants, adding they are "going to run for a while."
Smith and Wagoner met with reporters after accepting awards from J.D. Power and Associates.

Commenting on ongoing talks with the United Auto Workers in the United States, Smith said GM is involved in a "constructive dialogue" with the UAW. He said he would like to reach an agreement with the UAW as soon as possible, but does not want to sacrifice the company's ability to improve its competitiveness.

"If we could make the adjustments we need to make to take care of competitiveness issues that are presented to General Motors, because we're a very different company than Ford and Chrysler, we would like to have that happen as soon as possible."
Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp have agreed to new labor contracts with UAW that call for the companies to guarantee 95 percent of their current UAW workforces.
